notes.title: Chapter map: Iterators, generators & comprehensions
notes.html:
Every note in this chapter is a way to produce or consume a one-shot position. Read each arrow as a sentence: generators is-a iterator protocol.

Green = CORE, blue = SUPPORTING, yellow = BREADTH, grey = another chapter (dashed edges).

Reading order: 14 iterator protocol ─▶ 15 generators ─▶ 16 yield from ─▶ 17 send / throw / close ─▶ 18 comprehensions ─▶ 19 itertools

  • The one big idea: the iterable holds the data, the iterator holds the position. A generator is the shortest way to write an iterator, a genexp is the shortest way to write a generator, and itertools chains them because they all speak the same two calls, iter() and next().
  • The two most-confused pairs: iterable vs iterator vs generator (14: iter(x) is x, and its class diagram) · [...] vs (...): built now and reusable vs built on demand and one-shot (18).
  • Ten minutes before an interview: the ⚡ TL;DR, 🧭 Flow and ✏️ Draw-by-hand rows of 14 and 15, then the Break it in 14 (a container that is its own iterator).
  • Cross-chapter: dunder protocols (lookup on the type) · closures (keep variables, not execution) · async / await (the same parked frame, driven by an event loop).

No decision tree: these notes build on each other rather than being alternatives to choose between.

notes.title: The Iterator Protocol
notes.html:
📚 References

📘 Iterator types · 📘 iter() and the sentinel form · 📘 Glossary: iterator · 📜 PEP 479: StopIteration inside generators · 📖 Real Python: Iterators and iterables

⚡ TL;DR

The iterable holds the data; the iterator holds the position. iter() hands out a new bookmark; next() moves it forward and never back.

🧭 Flow: for x in nums ─▶ iter(nums) ─▶ new list_iterator (index 0) ─next() × n─▶ items ─▶ StopIteration ─▶ loop ends, nums untouched

🎯 Recall

Prompt Answer
Iterable vs iterator? Iterable: __iter__ returns an iterator. Iterator: __next__, plus __iter__ returning self.
What does for compile to? GET_ITER once (__iter__), then FOR_ITER per pass (__next__).
Where does the position live? On the iterator, never the iterable, so iterables are reusable.
What else consumes an iterator? in, list(), sum/max/any, zip, unpacking, *args.
iter(f, sentinel)? Calls f() until it returns sentinel, e.g. chunked reads until b"".
✏️ Draw by hand: Iterable / Iterator / Generator Generator is-an Iterator is-an Iterable; list creates a list_iterator holding the index.

💡 The idea

Why can you loop a list twice, even two nested loops at once, but a generator comes back empty the second time? Ask Python for what a for loop asks for:

nums = [10, 20, 30]
it = iter(nums)                # ① a new list_iterator, index 0
next(it), next(it), next(it)   # ② → (10, 20, 30)
next(it)                       # ③ → StopIteration
list(it), list(nums)           # → ([], [10, 20, 30])

iter(nums) returned a new list_iterator, and that object holds the position. It's spent; the list isn't, because the list never stored a position at all.

Anything that pulls from an iterator moves it, not just for:

it = iter([1, 2, 3, 4, 5])
3 in it                        # → True
list(it)                       # → [4, 5]   (1, 2, 3 were consumed finding it)

The trade: separating the position from the data lets any number of loops share one collection, and it is also why the object holding the position is single-use.

⚙️ How it works

Three roles, and only two of them are ever in a for loop. Generator is-an Iterator is-an Iterable; a list is only an Iterable, and it creates iterators:

So the position (index) lives on list_iterator, never on list. Now the calls a for loop makes, in order:

iter() once, next() until it raises. The rules that make it behave:

Rule What actually happens
Compiled form In CPython 3.12: GET_ITER (the type's tp_iter slot) once, FOR_ITER (tp_iternext) per pass. Built-in iterators end by returning NULL, no StopIteration object; your __next__ must raise one.
Lookup goes through the type iter() finds __iter__ on type(obj), so obj.__iter__ = … on an instance changes nothing. No __iter__ but a __getitem__? A legacy iterator indexes from 0 until IndexError.
An iterator's __iter__ returns self Every consumer calls iter() first. Returning self means "you already hold the bookmark", so a half-used iterator isn't silently rewound.
iter() checks the result __iter__ returning a list raises TypeError: iter() returned non-iterator of type 'list'.
Two-argument form iter(callable, sentinel) calls until the sentinel comes back: "call until X" becomes an iterator.

💻 Code

A reusable container hands out a fresh iterator per loop; a stream reads in bounded chunks:

class Page:
    """One page of API results: reusable, because the position isn't stored here."""
    def __init__(self, rows):
        self._rows = rows
    def __iter__(self):
        return iter(self._rows)         # fresh bookmark per loop; or: yield from self._rows

page = Page(["a", "b", "c"])
print(list(page), list(page))           # → ['a', 'b', 'c'] ['a', 'b', 'c']

def chunks(path, size=64 * 1024):
    with open(path, "rb") as f:         # closed even if the consumer stops early
        yield from iter(lambda: f.read(size), b"")   # b"" is the EOF sentinel

Memory stays at one chunk however big the file is.

⚠️ Break it: make the container its own iterator.

class Batch:
    def __init__(self, data): self.data, self.i = data, 0
    def __iter__(self): return self             # ❌ the container IS the bookmark
    def __next__(self):
        if self.i >= len(self.data): raise StopIteration
        self.i += 1
        return self.data[self.i - 1]
b = Batch([1, 2, 3])
print(list(b), list(b), len(b.data))
# look for: second list empty while b.data still holds 3 items
# naive model predicts: [1, 2, 3] [1, 2, 3] 3

On CPython 3.12 it prints [1, 2, 3] [] 3. Reusability isn't a property of holding data; it comes from __iter__ handing out a new position each time.

🗣️ Interview

30-second answer: An iterable can produce an iterator: it has __iter__, and each call returns a fresh one. An iterator does the stepping: __next__ returns the next item or raises StopIteration, and its __iter__ returns self. The position lives on the iterator, so a list loops any number of times but an iterator, including every generator, is one-shot. for is iter() once and next() until StopIteration.

Q · Mechanism — Walk me through exactly what for x in obj: does. It calls iter(obj), which looks up __iter__ on the type, falls back to __getitem__ indexing, and rejects a result without __next__. The iterator sits on the value stack, invisible to you; in CPython that's one GET_ITER. Each pass is a FOR_ITER: call __next__, bind, run the body. Exhaustion, a raised StopIteration or a C-level NULL, jumps past the body and never reaches your code.

Q · Failure — A generator looped twice is empty the second time; an if item in stream: check loses records; removing items from a list while looping skips some. Explain all three. The first two are one mechanism: the generator and the stream are iterators, so the first pull drives them forward for good (see the idea section). The third is the index story: a list iterator holds an integer into a live list, so remove shifts elements left while the index moves right, and the element after each removal is skipped with no error. Dicts and sets raise RuntimeError on size change; lists don't. Fix: list() once when it fits, re-create per pass, or iterate a copy.

Q · Design — Load multi-gigabyte JSONL exports into Postgres on a 512 MB worker. How does the protocol shape it, and where does it break? The binding constraint is that the file never fits, so the path is a chain of pulls: file lines → parse → validate (bad rows to a dead-letter file) → batch of 1,000 → COPY. Memory is one batch, and the database sets the pace. It breaks wherever a record is needed twice: retries can't re-loop a single-pass source, so checkpoint the byte offset per committed batch; global dedup in a set reintroduces unbounded memory, so push it to ON CONFLICT. Watch worker RSS first: flat after warm-up is healthy, a climb means some stage is accumulating.

⚖️ Compare

Iterable (list, dict, str, range) Iterator (iter(list), generator, map, zip, file)
Implements __iter__ (or legacy __getitem__) __next__ and __iter__ returning self
Holds the position no yes
Reusable yes, fresh iterator per iter() no, one-shot
iter(x) is x False True
len() / indexing usually never

🚫 Pitfalls

  • ❌ "A list is an iterator"
    ✅ A list is an iterable: __iter__, but no __next__.
    ↳ Proof: next([1, 2]) raises TypeError.
    ↳ Why it matters: each loop gets a fresh list_iterator, which is why a list loops twice and a generator doesn't.
  • 🪞 "x in something is a read-only check"
    ✅ Only on a container (it calls __contains__).
    ↳ On an iterator: it pulls items until it finds a match, and everything pulled is gone for the next reader.
  • 🔀 Not the same: iterable, iterator, generator
    ↳ Nesting: every generator is an iterator, every iterator is an iterable, not the reverse (see the class diagram).
    ↳ Test: iter(x) is x is True for a one-shot bookmark, False for a reusable source.
  • ❌ "If it loops, it's an Iterable"
    ✅ __getitem__-only classes loop but fail the ABC check.
    ↳ Why: collections.abc.Iterable only looks for __iter__.
    ↳ Reliable test: call iter(x) inside a try.
  • ⚠️ Don't return self from a container's __iter__.
    ↳ Why: the collection becomes a one-shot stream; the second loop is empty and nested loops corrupt each other (see Break it).
    ↳ Instead: return iter(self._items), or make __iter__ a generator.
  • ⚠️ Don't pass an iterator where len(), indexing or two passes are needed.
    ↳ Symptom: a two-pass helper silently returns wrong answers.
    ↳ Instead: annotate Iterable[T] (loop once) vs Sequence[T] (need more); see type hints.
  • 🔖 Version: GET_ITER / FOR_ITER / END_FOR is 3.12 bytecode.
    ↳ Expect differences: no END_FOR before 3.12; FOR_ITER_LIST appears after warm-up (3.11+).

🕸️ Connections

Path: dunder protocols ─▶ iterator protocol ─▶ generators ─▶ yield from ─▶ itertools

  • Builds on dunder protocols: iter() and next() look up __iter__ / __next__ on the type.
  • Builds on names & binding: two names on one iterator share one position.
  • Used by generators, genexps and itertools: all built on iter() / next(), which is why they chain.
  • Contrasts with async iteration: same shape (__aiter__ / __anext__), but each step is awaited.
  • Same idea elsewhere: Java's Iterable / Iterator, the JS iterator protocol, a database cursor.

notes.title: Generators & Lazy Evaluation
notes.html:
📚 References

📘 Yield expressions · 📘 Generator-iterator methods · 📜 PEP 255: Simple generators · 📜 PEP 479: StopIteration inside generators · 📖 Real Python: Generators and yield

⚡ TL;DR

A function's frame dies when it returns; a generator's frame pauses at yield. Calling it runs nothing; next() runs to the next yield; running off the end raises StopIteration.

🧭 Flow: g = gen() (nothing runs) ─next(g)─▶ body runs to yield v ─▶ v handed out, frame parked ─next(g)─▶ resumes after the yield ─▶ … ─▶ body ends ─▶ StopIteration, closed for good

🎯 Recall

Prompt Answer
What does calling a generator function do? Builds a generator object, frame parked before line 1. Runs nothing.
What survives a yield? The whole frame: locals, position, eval stack, open try/with blocks.
return x in a generator? Becomes StopIteration(x); for discards x, yield from captures it.
PEP 479? A StopIteration escaping the body becomes RuntimeError (default since 3.7).
When does a generator's finally run? Exhaustion, close(), or finalisation (immediate on CPython when the last ref drops).
✏️ Draw by hand: the generator lifecycle CREATED ─next─▶ RUNNING ─yield─▶ SUSPENDED ─next─▶ RUNNING ─end / close─▶ CLOSED

💡 The idea

A normal function runs at once, to the end, then its frame is destroyed; anything that survives must be in the return value. So producing a sequence means producing all of it, which for a 20 GB log is an OOMKill. Put yield in the body and the rules change:

def countdown(n):
    print("start")
    while n > 0:
        yield n
        n -= 1
    print("done")

g = countdown(3)          # ① → nothing printed: the body didn't run
next(g)                   # ② ③ → start · 3
next(g)                   # ④ → 2       (no second "start": it resumed after yield)
g.gi_frame.f_locals       # → {'n': 2}
list(g), list(g)          # ⑤ → done · ([1], [])

The local n survived between calls because the frame did. When the body runs off the end it raises StopIteration and stays finished, like any iterator.

The trade: you give up the whole result at once, and in exchange the frame outlives the call, so it hands you one value at a time and remembers exactly where it was.

⚙️ How it works

A generator is a frame that doesn't get thrown away. inspect.getgeneratorstate(g) reports which of four states it's in, as GEN_CREATED … GEN_CLOSED (transitions verified on CPython 3.12):

Four rules decide how it behaves in those states:

Rule What actually happens
Decided at compile time yield anywhere in a body sets a generator flag on the code object, so even an unreachable if False: yield makes a generator. A function is never "sometimes" a generator.
The whole frame survives a yield Locals, bytecode position, half-computed stack values, open try/with blocks (see the picture). In CPython 3.11+ the frame data lives inside the generator object, so suspending copies nothing.
return ends; it doesn't return return "val" becomes StopIteration("val"). PEP 479 turns a StopIteration escaping the body into RuntimeError, because before 3.7 a stray next(inner) silently ended the outer loop.
Cleanup has three triggers Exhaustion, close() (raises GeneratorExit at the paused yield), or finalisation. In CPython finalisation is usually immediate when the last reference drops; a lingering reference, a cycle or PyPy defers it.

💻 Code

A memory-bounded pipeline. Values are pulled from the right, so one record and one batch are in flight whatever the file size: bulk_insert ◀─ batched ◀─ read_records ◀─ file.

import json
from contextlib import closing

def read_records(path):
    with open(path) as f:                  # open across yields; closed when the gen is
        for line in f:
            yield json.loads(line)

def batched(rows, size):                   # 3.12+: itertools.batched (yields tuples)
    batch = []
    for row in rows:                       # pulls upstream only when asked
        batch.append(row)
        if len(batch) == size:
            yield batch
            batch = []
    if batch:
        yield batch                        # don't lose the last partial batch

with closing(batched(read_records("events.jsonl"), 500)) as batches:
    for batch in batches:
        db.bulk_insert(batch)              # slow sink throttles the reader: backpressure
        if shutdown_requested():
            break                          # closing() → close() → file closed now

closing makes cleanup deterministic on any exit instead of relying on finalisation.

⚠️ Break it: validation at the top of a generator.

def read_config(path):
    if not path:
        raise ValueError("path is required")
    with open(path) as f:
        yield from f
g = read_config("")
print("created OK:", g)
next(g)
# look for: "created OK" prints; ValueError only at next(g)
# naive model predicts: ValueError on the read_config("") line

On CPython 3.12 it prints created OK: <generator object …>, then the traceback comes from next(g). The body, checks included, runs on the first pull, so split it: an eager function validates, then returns an inner generator.

🗣️ Interview

30-second answer: A function with yield compiles to a generator function. Calling it runs nothing; it returns a generator whose frame is parked before the first line. Each next() runs to the next yield, hands out the value and suspends with locals and position intact. You get lazy, O(1)-memory production and an iterator without a class. The cost: it's one-shot, has no len(), and its setup code runs late.

Q · Mechanism — How does a generator suspend and resume, and what's preserved? The generator owns a frame. At yield it hands out the value and parks the frame, position and open blocks included, inside the generator object instead of destroying it; next() pushes it back on the stack and continues (the picture, then the state diagram). A closure keeps only variables; a generator keeps the whole call. That's why finally works inside one: close() raises GeneratorExit at the paused yield.

Q · Failure — A generator pipeline sometimes leaks file handles, and a refactored generator silently truncated output on an old runtime. Diagnose both. The leak is cleanup timing: the file closes on exhaustion, close() or finalisation. Tests pass because CPython finalises at once when a for loop held the only reference; production leaks when a reference outlives the loop (stored on an object, in a traceback, in a cycle) or on PyPy. Fix: contextlib.closing. The truncation is pre-3.7 PEP 479 behaviour: a bare next(inner) leaked StopIteration and the consumer read it as "done". Use next(inner, default).

Q · Design — A streaming ETL stage reads an unbounded source on a memory-constrained worker. How do generators shape it, and where do they stop being enough? Bounded memory against an unbounded source binds, so it's source → parse → transform → batched → write, O(batch) in flight, and the pull model gives backpressure for free. Cleanup (commit offset, flush partial batch) goes in finally, under closing. They stop at concurrency: the chain is synchronous, so one slow write stalls every stage. Next step: async generators, or a bounded queue between reader and writer threads; scale out by partitioning the source, since generators can't be pickled. Watch source lag against RSS first.

⚖️ Compare

Generator (yield) Function returning a list Iterator class
Runs lazily, per next() eagerly, at call lazily
Memory in flight O(1) O(n) O(1)
Reusable result no yes no
Infinite sequence yes never returns yes
State lives in suspended frame nowhere attributes
Best for streams, pipelines small, reused, indexed results extra methods, pickling

🚫 Pitfalls

  • ❌ "Calling a generator runs it up to the first yield"
    ✅ Calling it runs nothing; the body starts on the first next().
    ↳ Symptom: a bad argument raises far from the call, often in another function or a background task (see Break it).
  • 🪞 "A generator's finally only runs if the loop finishes"
    ✅ It also runs on close() and on garbage collection.
    ↳ Real risk: a reference that outlives the loop delays cleanup indefinitely (rule table: cleanup).
  • ❌ "return value in a generator gives the caller that value"
    ✅ It ends the generator inside StopIteration.
    ↳ So: for and list() throw it away; only yield from (or a manual catch) sees it.
  • 🔀 Not the same as a coroutine
    ↳ Difference: plain yield only sends values out; [[03-iterators-generators-comprehensions/17-coroutine-style-generators|send()]] brings them in.
    ↳ Also: async def coroutines are a separate type that next() can't drive, though both use the same suspended frame.
  • ⚠️ Don't rely on garbage collection to close resources inside a generator.
    ↳ Why: a stored reference, a traceback or a cycle keeps it alive; PyPy doesn't collect promptly at all.
    ↳ Instead: contextlib.closing(gen) or an explicit close().
  • ⚠️ Don't share one generator between threads.
    ↳ Symptom: concurrent next() raises ValueError: generator already executing or interleaves items.
    ↳ Instead: a queue.Queue between producer and consumers.
  • 🔖 Version: PEP 479 (leaked StopIteration → RuntimeError) is the default since 3.7.
    ↳ Also: frame inside the generator object is a CPython 3.11+ detail; itertools.batched 3.12+, strict= in 3.13.

🕸️ Connections

Path: iterator protocol ─▶ generators ─▶ yield from ─▶ send / throw / close ─▶ async / await

  • Builds on the iterator protocol: a generator is an iterator whose __next__ resumes a frame (see its class diagram).
  • Contrasts with closures: a closure keeps variables in cells; a generator keeps the whole running call.
  • Used by generator expressions and itertools: lazy stages that chain because each one pulls from the last.
  • Same mechanism as async coroutines: the same parked frame, resumed by an event loop instead of next().
  • Breaks when combined with threads and multiprocessing: one frame can't run twice at once, and it can't be pickled.

notes.title: yield from & Generator Delegation
notes.html:
📚 References

📘 Yield expressions · 📜 PEP 380: Delegating to a subgenerator · 📖 Real Python: Generators and yield

⚡ TL;DR

for x in sub: yield x forwards values out. yield from sub forwards everything, both ways, and hands back sub's return value.

🧭 Flow: outer reaches yield from sub() and parks ─▶ next / send(v) / throw / close go straight to sub ─▶ sub's values come straight out ─▶ sub returns x ─▶ StopIteration(x) becomes the value of yield from ─▶ outer carries on

🎯 Recall

Prompt Answer
What does yield from add over a re-yield loop? Forwards send/throw/close to sub; evaluates to sub's return value.
How do you get a sub-generator's return value? result = yield from sub(), taken from StopIteration.value.
How deep does it flatten? One level; deep flattening needs recursive yield from.

💡 The idea

Is yield from sub just a shorter loop? For the values coming out, yes. But the loop is a middleman with its own frame, and the inner generator's return value dies in it:

def subgen():
    yield "a"; yield "b"
    return "done"

def outer():
    result = yield from subgen()       # with a for loop, "done" is swallowed
    print("captured:", result)
    yield from ["p", "q"]              # any iterable works

list(outer())                          # → captured: done · ['a', 'b', 'p', 'q']

The other direction matters more. With a loop, g.send("x") lands on the outer generator's yield, where nobody reads it, and the inner generator gets None. With yield from, the send reaches the inner generator directly, and so do throw() and close() (send / throw / close).

The trade: you lose the middleman's chance to inspect each value, and in exchange the outer generator becomes a transparent pipe in both directions, with the inner result handed back at the end.

⚙️ How it works

While delegating, the outer frame is a parked pipe (verified on CPython 3.12):

The outer frame doesn't run during delegation. It's parked on the yield from line (CPython: outer.gi_yieldfrom points at sub). throw(E) raises at sub's paused yield; close() closes sub, then raises GeneratorExit in the outer frame.

The result comes from the exception. sub's StopIteration.value becomes the expression's value. An unhandled exception in sub surfaces at the yield from line, where a normal try can catch it. A plain list has nothing to send into, so it just iterates.

await is the same pipe. Pre-3.5 asyncio coroutines were generators that waited with result = yield from other(), so the event loop could drive the innermost one; PEP 492 gave it its own syntax (async / await).

💻 Code

Recursive traversal, where each level delegates one level down:

def walk(node, path=()):
    """Depth-first over nested config, yielding (path, leaf) lazily."""
    if isinstance(node, dict):
        for key, child in node.items():
            yield from walk(child, path + (key,))   # delegate to the subtree
    elif isinstance(node, list):
        for i, child in enumerate(node):
            yield from walk(child, path + (i,))
    else:
        yield path, node

cfg = {"db": {"host": "pg", "ports": [5432, 6432]}, "debug": False}
print(list(walk(cfg)))
# → [(('db', 'host'), 'pg'), (('db', 'ports', 0), 5432), (('db', 'ports', 1), 6432), (('debug',), False)]

Each nesting level is one more suspended frame, so very deep trees can hit the recursion limit.

🗣️ Interview

30-second answer: For values out, yield from sub equals a re-yield loop. The difference is everything else: send() reaches the inner generator, throw() raises inside it, close() closes it first, and its return value becomes the expression's value. That two-way transparency is what generator-based asyncio was built on, and await is its coroutine-only descendant.

Q · Mechanism — What exactly does yield from forward, and why did it matter for asyncio? While the outer generator is parked, next/send resume sub, throw raises at its yield, and close closes it and then the outer frame. Yields go straight to the outer caller, and sub's return becomes the expression. In 3.4 asyncio, a coroutine was a generator and yield from other() meant "wait for it", so the loop talking to the outermost coroutine was really driving the one waiting on a socket. Cancellation still travels this way: CancelledError is thrown down the chain of awaits.

⚖️ Compare

for x in sub: yield x yield from sub await aw
Values out yes yes suspensions go to the loop
send/throw/close reach inner no yes throw yes (cancellation)
Inner's return value discarded expression value expression value
Can transform each item yes no no

🚫 Pitfalls

  • ❌ "yield from is only a shorter loop"
    ✅ Same values out, but it also forwards send, throw, close and returns the inner return value.
    ↳ Symptom: swapping one for the other changes behaviour as soon as anything is sent in.
  • ❌ "yield from flattens any nesting"
    ✅ It delegates to exactly one iterable.
    ↳ Proof: yield from [[1, 2], [3]] yields the two lists, not 1, 2, 3.
    ↳ Fix: recurse, one level per call.
  • 🔀 Not the same as await
    ↳ Difference: same delegation mechanism, but yield from takes any iterable in a plain generator; await takes awaitables only, inside async def.
    ↳ So: yield from for I/O is the pre-3.5 style.
  • ⚠️ Don't use yield from when you need to filter, map or count items.
    ↳ Why: it gives you no hook per item.
    ↳ Instead: a for loop with yield.
  • ⚠️ Don't drop a meaningful return value.
    ↳ Why: a bare yield from sub() discards what sub returned (a count, a checksum).
    ↳ Fix: result = yield from sub().
  • 🔖 Version: yield from is 3.3+ (PEP 380); @asyncio.coroutine deprecated 3.8, removed 3.11.
    ↳ Also: yield from is a syntax error inside async def, so old coroutine code needs rewriting.

🕸️ Connections

Path: generators ─▶ yield from ─▶ send / throw / close ─▶ async / await

  • Builds on generators: return x inside a generator becomes StopIteration(x), which is what yield from catches.
  • Used by coroutine-style generators: delegation is what makes send and throw reach the right frame.
  • Same mechanism as await: the same transparent pipe, with its own keyword and type since 3.5.
  • Contrasts with a for x in sub: yield x loop: values out only; sends land on the wrong yield, and the return value is lost.
  • Same idea elsewhere: JavaScript's yield* delegates to another generator and evaluates to its return value.

notes.title: Coroutine-Style Generators (.send() / .throw() / .close())
notes.html:
📚 References

📘 Generator-iterator methods · 📜 PEP 342: Coroutines via enhanced generators

⚡ TL;DR

yield sends a value out; send() sends one back in through the same yield. Prime with next(), inject with throw(), finish with close().

🎯 Recall

Prompt Answer
What does gen.send(v) do? Resumes; the paused yield evaluates to v; returns the next yielded value.
Why prime with next()? A fresh generator isn't at a yield; non-None send raises TypeError.
throw() vs close()? throw(E) raises E at the pause; close() raises GeneratorExit so cleanup runs.

💡 The idea

yield is an expression: x = yield avg sends avg out, and the next send(10) makes it evaluate to 10. You get a stateful consumer with no class. Prime it first, or send raises TypeError: can't send non-None value to a just-started generator. Swallowing GeneratorExit and yielding again raises RuntimeError. This is the groundwork async/await was built on.

💻 Code

def running_average():
    total = count = 0; avg = None
    while True:
        x = yield avg          # avg goes OUT; the next send() comes IN as x
        total += x; count += 1; avg = total / count
acc = running_average(); next(acc)                 # prime: run to the first yield
print(acc.send(10), acc.send(20), acc.send(30))    # → 10.0 15.0 20.0

notes.title: Comprehensions & Generator Expressions
notes.html:
📚 References

📘 Displays for lists, sets and dictionaries · 📜 PEP 709: Inlined comprehensions · 📜 PEP 572: Assignment expressions · 📖 GeeksforGeeks: List comprehension

⚡ TL;DR

[...] builds it now; (...) builds it when asked, once. The loop variable stays inside; only the walrus gets out.

🧭 Flow: first iterable evaluated at once, in the enclosing scope ─▶ [...]: every element computed now, into a list ─▶ (...): a generator, each element computed on the next next() ─▶ loop variable lives in the comprehension's own scope ─▶ only a := target escapes

🎯 Recall

Prompt Answer
[...] vs (...)? List built now, O(n); lazy one-shot generator, O(1).
Does the loop variable leak? No, own scope; only a walrus (:=) target escapes.
Why does [base * n for n in r] fail in a class body? Only the first iterable sees class scope.

💡 The idea

A for loop builds its list now and leaves its loop variable behind, clobbering any outer name. A comprehension doesn't, and changing the brackets changes eager into lazy:

nums, x = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6], "outer"
[x * x for x in nums if x % 2 == 0], x      # → ([4, 16, 36], 'outer')
lazy = (x * x for x in nums if x % 2 == 0)
sum(lazy), sum(lazy)                        # → (56, 0)   one-shot
[y for v in [1, 5, 2, 8] if (y := v * 10) > 30], y   # → ([50, 80], 80)

Parentheses make a generator expression, not a tuple. The walrus is the deliberate exception to the private scope: it binds in the enclosing function.

When each element is actually computed, with def f(x): print("f", x); return x (traced on CPython 3.12):

Step Code Printed Why
1 L = [f(x) for x in range(3)] f 0 · f 1 · f 2 eager: the whole list is built now
2 G = (f(x) for x in range(3)) — lazy: only range(3) runs
3 next(G) f 0 one element on demand
4 next(G) f 1 resumes where it parked
5 (x for x in missing) NameError at creation the first iterable is never deferred

The trade: a private scope and a single expression in exchange for no statements inside, and the brackets are where you choose eager or lazy.

⚙️ How it works

The first iterable is evaluated at once, even in a genexp. In (f(x) for x in source), source is evaluated on the spot in the enclosing scope; everything else waits and is looked up in the comprehension's own scope. So (x for x in missing) raises NameError immediately.

That split is the class-body trap. A class body isn't an enclosing scope for nested code (LEGB), so a class attribute works in the first iterable and nowhere else in the comprehension.

3.12 changed the implementation, not the rules. PEP 709 inlines list, set and dict comprehensions into the enclosing bytecode instead of a hidden function, so there's no extra frame. Generator expressions keep theirs because they must suspend.

💻 Code

Each line picks its shape on purpose:

rows = fetch_rows()                                        # list of dicts
active_ids  = [r["id"] for r in rows if r["active"]]       # list: used twice below
by_id       = {r["id"]: r for r in rows}                   # dict: O(1) lookup
tenants     = {r["tenant"] for r in rows}                  # set: dedupe
total_bytes = sum(r["size"] for r in rows)                 # genexp: no temp list
has_error   = any(r["status"] == "error" for r in rows)    # genexp: stops at first hit
parsed = [p for r in rows if (p := parse(r["payload"])) is not None]   # parse once

Without the walrus, parse() runs twice per row: once to filter, once to output.

🗣️ Interview

30-second answer: A comprehension builds a list, set or dict in its own scope, so the loop variable doesn't leak; only a walrus target does. Parentheses give a generator expression: lazy, O(1) memory, one-shot. Use a genexp when the result is consumed once, especially into sum, any or join; use a list when you need len(), indexing or two passes, or want errors at the line that built it.

Q · Mechanism — Why doesn't the loop variable leak, and where does that scope bite? The variables are local to the comprehension (How it works). It bites three ways: the class-body trap, where only the first iterable sees class attributes; lambdas made inside, which close over the variable, so [lambda: i for i in range(3)] all return 2 (fix: lambda i=i: i); and the walrus, which deliberately binds outside.

⚖️ Compare

List [...] Set {...} Dict {k: v} Genexp (...)
Computed now now now per next()
Memory O(n) O(n) O(n) O(1)
Reusable yes yes yes no
Inlined in 3.12+ yes yes yes no, own frame
Best for reuse, indexing uniqueness lookup by key aggregate once, short-circuit

🚫 Pitfalls

  • ❌ "Parentheses make a tuple"
    ✅ (x for x in xs) is a generator expression: lazy and one-shot.
    ↳ Symptom: looks like a tuple in review; a second loop later gets nothing.
    ↳ Fix: tuple(x for x in xs).
  • ❌ "A generator expression evaluates nothing until consumed"
    ✅ Its first iterable is evaluated immediately, in the enclosing scope.
    ↳ Proof: (x for x in missing) raises NameError on that line; (missing for x in [1]) waits until next().
  • 🔀 Not the same: list comp vs genexp
    ↳ Difference: eager vs lazy, not just syntax.
    ↳ Both ways wrong: a list comp over a huge stream brings back O(n) memory; a genexp given to two-pass code silently empties the second pass.
  • ⚠️ Don't write comprehensions for side effects.
    ↳ Why: [send(x) for x in batch] builds a throwaway list of None and hides the point.
    ↳ Instead: a plain for loop.
  • ⚠️ Don't nest more than two for/if clauses.
    ↳ Why: clauses read left to right like nested loops, which few people parse correctly at a glance.
    ↳ Instead: write the loop.
  • 🔖 Version: walrus 3.8+ (PEP 572); list/set/dict comprehensions inlined in 3.12 (PEP 709).
    ↳ So: no <listcomp> frame in tracebacks, and locals() inside one includes the enclosing names.

🕸️ Connections

Path: generators ─▶ comprehensions & genexps ─▶ itertools

  • Is a generator, when written with parentheses: one-shot, lazy, its own frame.
  • Builds on LEGB: a comprehension has its own scope, which is why the loop variable doesn't leak.
  • Used by itertools pipelines: genexps are the usual first and middle stages.
  • Contrasts with a for loop: statements allowed, eager, and the loop variable leaks into the enclosing scope.
  • Same idea elsewhere: Haskell list comprehensions (lazy by default) and C# LINQ queries (deferred until enumerated).

notes.title: itertools & functools.reduce Patterns
notes.html:
📚 References

📘 itertools · 📘 functools.reduce

⚡ TL;DR

A list stage builds the whole result; an itertools stage yields one item when asked. groupby needs sorted input; tee buffers the gap; reduce needs an initial value.

🎯 Recall

Prompt Answer
The groupby trap? Groups only adjacent equal keys; sort by the same key first.
batched / pairwise versions? batched 3.12+ (yields tuples); pairwise 3.10+.
Why give reduce an initial value? Empty input otherwise raises TypeError.

💡 The idea

Chaining, slicing, grouping and batching with lists materialises every stage. itertools does the same jobs as lazy iterator-to-iterator adapters (chain, islice, groupby, batched, pairwise, accumulate, tee, product), so stages compose at O(1) memory each. reduce is the eager end that folds a stream to one value. You lose random access and reuse; tee buffers whatever one branch has seen and another hasn't.

💻 Code

import itertools as it; from functools import reduce; from operator import itemgetter, mul
rows = [("a", 1), ("b", 2), ("a", 3)]
print([(k, [v for _, v in g]) for k, g in it.groupby(rows, key=itemgetter(0))])
# → [('a', [1]), ('b', [2]), ('a', [3])]   unsorted: 'a' split in two
print([(k, [v for _, v in g]) for k, g in it.groupby(sorted(rows), key=itemgetter(0))])
# → [('a', [1, 3]), ('b', [2])]
print(list(it.batched(range(7), 3)), reduce(mul, [1, 2, 3, 4], 1))
# → [(0, 1, 2), (3, 4, 5), (6,)] 24
